passage: Rain had pushed the whole PE class into the school hall, where forty children were shouting over the thunder. In one corner, Preeti and Vijay were nose to nose over the one dry football, Vijay's fists clenched, Preeti close to tears. Mrs D'Souza didn't ask who started it. She stepped between them. "Vijay, fill your bottle at the cooler and walk back slowly. Preeti, sit by the window with me and take ten slow breaths." The buses were due in fifteen minutes, and she could easily have made a quick ruling. She waited instead. When Vijay came back with his shoulders down, she asked each of them what had happened, and then, "What were you feeling right then?"

qa.q: Why was the PE class in the school hall?
qa.a: Rain had pushed the whole PE class into the school hall.

qa.q: What does Vijay's posture suggest about how he felt after his walk?
qa.a: He came back with his shoulders down instead of fists clenched, which suggests the anger had drained.

qa.q: Why did waiting work better than a quick ruling, even with the buses due?
qa.a: A quick ruling would have left one child feeling cheated and still upset; cooling down first meant both could explain and share feelings.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt when the teacher asked about feelings instead of blame?
qa.a: Preeti may have felt relieved to be listened to rather than judged, which makes it easier to talk honestly. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teacher separating two children and letting each cool down with water or breathing before asking for their version and feelings.

passage: The tuition room in Manjula Miss's Jayanagar flat was small, and the fight over the shared ruler filled it. Shreya had snapped it; Nitin said she did it on purpose; Shreya called him a liar. Manjula Miss put down her chai. "Right. No one is in trouble. Shreya, walk out to the balcony and water the tulsi. Nitin, drink this glass of water, slowly." Neither child moved at first. Then Shreya stomped out, and Nitin gulped, then sipped. Two minutes passed. The traffic horns below filled the silence. When Shreya came back, her breathing had slowed. Manjula Miss sat between them. "Now. Tell me what happened, one at a time. And tell me how it felt inside."

qa.q: What did Manjula Miss ask Shreya to do?
qa.a: She asked Shreya to walk out to the balcony and water the tulsi.

qa.q: Why did Manjula Miss say "No one is in trouble" first?
qa.a: She wanted both children to stop feeling they had to defend themselves, so they could calm down before anything else.

qa.q: What order of steps does Manjula Miss follow, and why does it help?
qa.a: First separate and cool down with water and a small task, then hear each version and the feelings; calm first makes listening possible.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel about the teacher not deciding who was right about the ruler?
qa.a: Nitin might feel a little frustrated at first, but also safer, because nobody is being declared the winner or the liar.

grounding: Shows an adult pausing a quarrel without judging, letting each child cool down, then asking for their version and feelings.

"Stop. Both of you. Hands down." Gargi Ma'am stepped between them in the corridor.
"She started it!" Madhuri cried.
"I didn't ask who started it. Madhuri, go to the water cooler and drink a full glass, slowly. Tenzin, walk to the end of the corridor and back, twice."
"But Ma'am, she—"
"Later. Water first."
Five minutes passed. Madhuri came back with wet sleeves and slower breathing.
"Better?" Ma'am asked. Madhuri nodded.
"Now tell me what happened, and what you were feeling when it happened."
"I felt stupid when Tenzin laughed at my drawing."
"Thank you. Tenzin, your turn next."

qa.q: What did Gargi Ma'am ask Madhuri to do first?
qa.a: She asked Madhuri to go to the water cooler and drink a full glass, slowly.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling underneath the fight, according to what she says once calmer?
qa.a: She felt stupid and hurt when Tenzin laughed at her drawing.

qa.q: Why did Gargi Ma'am's order of steps work?
qa.a: She separated them and let each cool down with water or a walk before asking questions, so they could explain instead of shouting.

qa.q: What might Tenzin be experiencing while walking the corridor?
qa.a: Tenzin may be cooling down but still worried about getting blamed, and is waiting for a turn to be heard.

grounding: A teacher separates two children without deciding who won, lets each cool down with water or a walk, then asks for their version and feelings.

passage:
I've taught Class 5 for eleven years, and the children call me Afreen Ma'am. The day I think about most is when Harish and another boy were rolling on the floor over a pencil box.
I didn't shout. I didn't ask who started it. I put one hand on each shoulder and said, "You go to the tap and wash your face. You walk once round the ground."
Harish glared at me. His whole body was shaking. But he went.
When he came back, dripping, I gave him a minute more. Only then I asked, "What happened, and what were you feeling?" He whispered, "Scared he'd break it. It was my brother's."
That was all I needed to hear first.

qa.q: How many years has Afreen Ma'am taught Class 5?
qa.a: She has taught Class 5 for eleven years.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling underneath the fight?
qa.a: He was scared and upset that the pencil box, which was his brother's, would get broken.

qa.q: What turning point did Afreen Ma'am create?
qa.a: She separated them without ruling on who started it and gave each a way to cool down, so that only when he was calm could Harish tell her what he felt.

qa.q: What might the other boy be experiencing while walking round the ground?
qa.a: He may be cooling off and a bit nervous about being blamed, but relieved that nobody decided against him yet.

grounding: A teacher recalls separating two fighting boys without judging, letting each cool down first, then asking for their story and feelings.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Thursday

I was passing Class 4 at break when Shreya and Vidya were shouting over the class plant they both look after. Ms Pillai, their class teacher, got there first.
She did not ask who was right. She sent Shreya to fill the watering can at the far tap and asked Vidya to help her carry books to the staffroom. Both went, still red-faced.
Ten minutes later the teacher sat each girl down separately and asked two things: what happened, and what were you feeling? Vidya said she felt left out of the plant chart.
I offered to join them on Monday to help plan the plant turns together. The teacher agreed.

qa.q: What were Shreya and Vidya shouting over?
qa.a: The class plant they both look after.

qa.q: What did Vidya say she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt left out of the plant chart.

qa.q: Why did Ms Pillai's approach help the girls?
qa.a: She separated them without ruling on who was right and gave each a calming task before asking for their version and feelings, so they could speak calmly.

qa.q: What might Shreya be experiencing while filling the watering can?
qa.a: She is probably still upset but slowly cooling down, and may be relieved she was not blamed in front of the class.

grounding: A counsellor records a teacher separating two girls without judging, letting them cool down, then asking each for their story and feelings.

passage:
Dear Diary,

Today Omkar and I had the biggest fight of Class 5. He said I copied his drawing for the competition. I didn't. I said he was a liar and he said I was one. We were both shouting and I was nearly crying.

Rawat Ma'am came. She didn't say who was right. She just said, "Dolma, go and fill your bottle. Omkar, walk to the gate and back." I was angry she didn't take my side.

When I came back I felt less hot. Ma'am sat with me first and asked what happened and how I felt. I said I felt blamed for nothing. Then she talked to Omkar alone.

I still don't like what he said. But my stomach doesn't hurt anymore.

Dolma

qa.q: What did Omkar say Dolma copied?
qa.a: Omkar said Dolma copied his drawing for the competition.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when Rawat Ma'am didn't take her side?
qa.a: Dolma felt angry and let down, wanting the teacher to say who was right.

qa.q: Why did Rawat Ma'am's approach work?
qa.a: She separated them and let each cool down first, then listened to each one's story and feelings, so they could talk calmly.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt walking to the gate and back?
qa.a: Omkar was probably still angry at first but calmer by the end, ready to tell his side when Ma'am talked to him alone.

grounding: A teacher separates two children without ruling on who won, lets each cool down, then asks each for their version and feelings.
